conceptTag: The Bay of Pigs and groupthink
readerTitle: The Bay of Pigs: how a room of smart people agreed on a bad plan
caseNote: 실제 사건 (1961년 피그스만 침공, 1962년 쿠바 미사일 위기) + 실제 연구 (Irving Janis의 집단사고) + 가상 적용 (회계법인)
insight: 집단사고는 똑똑한 사람이 부족해서가 아니라 반대 의견을 꺼내기 어려운 회의 방식에서 생긴다. 그래서 사람이 아니라 절차를 바꾸면 막을 수 있다.
misconception: 유능한 전문가들이 모두 찬성했다면 그 계획은 충분히 검증된 것이다. 회의에서 반대가 없으면 다들 동의한다는 뜻이다.

sources.text: Janis, I. L. (1972). Victims of Groupthink. Houghton Mifflin. (2nd ed. 1982, Groupthink). 피그스만 침공과 쿠바 미사일 위기 비교, 집단사고 증상
JFK Presidential Library, The Bay of Pigs (침공 개요, 병력 규모, 결과, 케네디의 책임 인정)
U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian, The Bay of Pigs Invasion and its Aftermath, April 1961–October 1962
Schlesinger, A. M. Jr. (1965). A Thousand Days. Houghton Mifflin. (회의에서 침묵한 것에 대한 회고)
Kennedy, R. F. (1969). Thirteen Days. W. W. Norton. (미사일 위기 당시 회의 방식)

factChecks.note: 침공 병력 '약 1,400명', 전투가 '약 3일'(1961년 4월 17~19일) 만에 끝났다는 점, 대부분 포로로 잡혔다는 점을 JFK 도서관과 국무부 역사실 자료로 확인하세요. 포로 수(1,100명 이상)는 카드에 숫자로 쓰지 않고 'most of the force'로만 적었습니다.
상륙 지점이 원래 계획(Trinidad 인근)에서 피그스만으로 옮겨져 산악 지대(Escambray)와 멀어지고 늪지대가 사이에 놓였다는 내용을 확인하세요. 카드에는 거리 수치 없이 'far from the mountains, across swamps'로만 적었습니다.
Schlesinger가 반대 메모를 썼지만 회의에서는 거의 말하지 않았고 나중에 이를 자책했다는 내용은 A Thousand Days와 Janis에 나옵니다. 직접 인용은 하지 않고 풀어 썼습니다.
Robert Kennedy가 Schlesinger에게 대통령이 이미 결정했으니 더 밀어붙이지 말라고 했다는 일화는 Schlesinger의 회고와 Janis에 근거합니다. 카드에 'reportedly'로 표시했습니다.
Fulbright 상원의원이 1961년 4월 초 회의에서 계획에 반대했다는 점을 확인하세요. 카드에는 날짜를 쓰지 않았습니다.
미사일 위기 때 케네디가 일부 회의에 일부러 빠졌고, Robert Kennedy와 Sorensen이 계획을 따지는 역할을 맡았으며, 여러 대안을 따로 검토했다는 내용은 Janis와 Thirteen Days로 확인하세요.
Janis의 해석에 대한 역사학계의 반론(CIA의 정보 왜곡, 전 정부에서 넘겨받은 계획, 관료 조직 요인 등)이 있다는 점은 일반적으로만 적었습니다.

cards.title: The Bay of Pigs: how a room of smart people agreed on a bad plan
body: In April 1961, about 1,400 Cuban exiles trained by the CIA landed at the Bay of Pigs in Cuba. Within about three days, the invasion had collapsed.
The plan had been approved by a new president and some of the most respected advisers in Washington. Several of them had doubts. Almost none said so in the room.

image.label: A long meeting table where everyone nods and one person stays silent
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 1960년대 분위기의 긴 회의 테이블, 대부분 사람이 고개를 끄덕이고 한 사람만 메모지를 쥔 채 말없이 앉아 있음. 실제 인물 얼굴, 국기, 정부 문장은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: It's April 1961. You lead the final meeting.
body: You are President Kennedy, three months into the job. The CIA's plan, inherited from the last administration: exiles land, Cubans rise up to join them, and if things go wrong the force escapes into the mountains. The U.S. role stays hidden.
Your senior advisers support it. One aide has sent you a private memo full of doubts. How do you run the final meeting?

options.text: Approve it. The experts who built the plan are confident
options.feedback: You save time and show trust. But the people who built a plan are the least likely to look for its weak spots.

options.text: Go around the table and ask each adviser for a yes or no
options.feedback: Everyone gets a turn, which helps. But when people know where the leader leans, a public vote mostly measures who wants to agree.

options.text: Assign someone to argue against it, and ask what happens if the uprising never comes
options.feedback: It costs time and some comfort. In return, doubts become a job instead of a risk, and the plan's key assumption gets tested.

cards.title: Every key assumption failed.
body: The landing site had been moved to the Bay of Pigs, far from the mountains, across swamps. Escape was no longer realistic.
No popular uprising came. The U.S. role was exposed almost at once. Most of the force was killed or captured.
Kennedy publicly took responsibility. Privately, the question was harder: how did so many capable people miss what now looked obvious?

cards.title: Groupthink
body: **Groupthink** is what happens when a close group values agreement so much that members stop testing the plan in front of them.

Psychologist Irving Janis made the Bay of Pigs his central case in his 1972 book *Victims of Groupthink*. His point was not that the advisers were foolish. It was that a confident, loyal, close-knit group created a room where doubting felt like disloyalty.

cards.title: Silence that looked like agreement.
body: Janis traced several warning signs in the room:
list: **Self-censorship:** adviser Arthur Schlesinger wrote memos against the plan but stayed mostly quiet in meetings, and later blamed himself
**Illusion of unanimity:** silence was read as a yes
**Mind guards:** Robert Kennedy reportedly told Schlesinger the president had decided, so stop pushing
**Outsiders ignored:** Senator Fulbright objected, but he wasn't part of the inner circle
cards.callout: No one forced agreement. The room did.
cards.softwareNote: In a product review, groupthink looks like a founder's pet feature that no one questions. Written comments collected before the meeting, read before the founder speaks, bring out doubts that would never be said aloud.

cards.title: Same people, different process.
body: In October 1962, many of the same advisers faced the Cuban Missile Crisis. This time Kennedy changed how they decided.
He stayed out of some meetings so people would speak freely. Robert Kennedy and Ted Sorensen were asked to challenge every proposal. Smaller groups worked up competing options before anyone chose.
Janis held up the contrast as proof: the cure for groupthink is not smarter people. It is a process that makes disagreement normal.

image.label: Two meeting diagrams: one leader at the center vs. several small groups with arrows of debate
image.brief: 좌우 비교 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 "1961": 리더를 중심으로 모두 같은 방향 화살표. 오른쪽 "1962": 작은 그룹 세 개가 서로 다른 안을 들고 화살표로 토론, 리더는 한쪽에서 듣는 모습. 실제 인물, 국기, 로고 없음.

cards.title: Groupthink isn't the whole story.
body: Historians point to other causes too: an inherited plan, CIA briefings that overstated the odds, and pressure to look tough. Groupthink explains part of the failure, not all of it.
The missile crisis also ended peacefully partly through luck. A better process improves your odds; it doesn't guarantee the outcome.
And forced dissent can become a ritual. A devil's advocate everyone knows is just playing a role is easy to ignore.

cards.title: Now it's an accounting firm.
body: You're the managing partner of a 25-person accounting firm. You want to win a large new client that would take most of your staff's time during tax season.
You present the idea to your four partners. They all nod. What do you do next?

options.text: Ask, "Any objections?" and move ahead if no one speaks
options.feedback: Fast and friendly. But after you've made the pitch, silence tells you more about the room than about the plan.

options.text: Have each partner write down the biggest risk before discussing, and name one to argue against it
options.feedback: It slows the decision by a meeting. In return, you hear about staffing and other clients before you sign, not after.

options.text: Ask your most senior partner for a gut check afterward
options.feedback: One honest view helps. But it's still one person, and your senior partner may feel the same pull to agree with you.

cards.title: When everyone agrees, check the room before the plan.
body: Groupthink grows in loyal, confident teams where doubting feels disloyal. The fix is a process: collect doubts before the leader speaks, and make challenging the plan someone's job.
**Try it today:** before your next big decision, ask everyone to write one reason it could fail, then read them aloud before you share your view.
